statement: The system shall keep end users' personal information organized in a way that makes sense to them.
The system shall preserve the user's information structure when users add, edit, delete, or back up data.
The system shall allow users to retrieve and manage their information easily across different kinds of content.
The system shall keep relationships created by users intact over time.
The system shall provide client application developers with a stable, application-independent framework that their applications can plug into to work with the same underlying information.
The system shall provide reliable API or services for client application developers.
The system shall allow client applications to access and manipulate data without requiring them to invent their own storage model.
The system shall be dependable, safe, and maintainable for administrators or support staff.
The system shall support smooth backups and recovery for administrators or support staff.
The system shall minimize the risk of data loss.
The system shall provide good performance.
The system shall support multiple clients or users without becoming fragile or hard to manage.
The framework shall support storing personal information in ZNIX.
The framework shall support modifying personal information in ZNIX.
The framework shall support backing up personal information in ZNIX.
The framework shall allow other applications to use the same personal information through the framework.
The core focus of the scope shall be the information management capabilities.
The framework shall support everyday users.
The framework shall support compatible client applications.
The system shall be flexible enough for users to organize personal information in ways that make sense to them.
People tend to use a mix of tools to store and organize personal information.
Copying the same item into multiple places creates inconsistency and makes backups and updates more painful.
ZNIX shall replace the scattered, app-specific way people manage information with one shared framework.
Users shall be able to reorganize items without losing the relationships and structure they have already built.
The system shall allow users to create custom relationships and groupings between items that match their own way of understanding the information.
The system shall provide basic item management capabilities.
The system shall support adding information items.
The system shall support searching information quickly.
The framework shall expose a clean interface for client applications to integrate without needing to understand the internal data storage details.
ZNIX should provide the main features desired from the user and integration side.
The system shall provide shared information storage with stable item management.
The system shall support custom relationships and hierarchies.
The system shall provide a client integration interface.
The system's core data model shall be dependable before backup and the client integration interface are delivered.
The system shall act as one reliable source of truth for the user's information.
Users shall be able to safely manage their information over time without losing what they have already built around it.
The system shall support a broad range of personal information objects, not just one content type.
The system shall support text notes and file attachments.
The system shall support contacts and reference records.
The framework shall remain flexible enough to handle new object types later without redesigning everything.
The system shall separate the core item container from type-specific content.
Every item shall have common metadata including identity, dates, tags, and relationships.
The system shall store ownership or source metadata for each item.
The system shall support item status values such as active, archived, and deleted.
The system shall allow some metadata to be optional depending on the item type.
Application developers who will integrate with ZNIX should be considered a valuable stakeholder group.
End users who manage a lot of personal information should be considered a valuable stakeholder group.
For broader deployment, support or operations people might also matter as stakeholders.
Users and client app teams should be prioritized first.
The system shall provide users with a single, flexible place to store and work with personal information.
The system shall allow users to keep different kinds of information together.
The system shall allow users to organize information in ways that make sense to them.
The system shall preserve a user's information structure when the user adds information, edits information, removes information, or backs it up.
The system shall solve the problem of information being trapped in separate applications or rigid file systems.
The system shall make the same information reusable across compatible tools.
The system shall avoid requiring users to duplicate data when switching applications.
The system shall avoid requiring users to reorganize data when switching applications.
An organization is stable if the relationships and hierarchy created by the user remain intact when individual items change.
Retrieval remains useful if users can reliably find the same item or set of related items after additions.
Retrieval remains useful if users can reliably find the same item or set of related items after edits.
Retrieval remains useful if users can reliably find the same item or set of related items after deletions.
Retrieval remains useful if users can reliably find the same item or set of related items after a restore from backup.
Retrieval remains useful if users do not have to rebuild their structure to find the same item or set of related items.
Stability means the framework should not break links or lose meaning when content changes.
A user should be able to keep working with the same categories and relationships over time.
Backups should restore the state in a predictable way.
The system should remain as application-independent as possible.
The system should not assume a specific database.
The system should not assume a specific operating system if that can be avoided.
ZNIX services must be usable by different compatible applications.
ZNIX must not force businesses into a single technology stack.
The system should support gradual adoption during rollout.
The system should work alongside existing tools.
The system should not require a big-bang replacement for rollout.
Platform limitations affecting sharing, backup, or interoperability are a serious concern.
The storage model for archived information shall be object-based.
Archived information shall not be forced into a flat document model or a rigid folder tree.
The exact physical storage format has not yet been decided.
The storage approach shall support retrieval, organization, and backup without losing the user’s structure or meaning.
The system shall support archiving.
The system shall support retrieval.
The system shall provide a service interface that allows compatible applications to access the same information without maintaining separate copies.
The system shall be reliable.
The system shall be easy to use.
The system shall remain responsive enough for use in normal workflows.
The initial scope shall exclude functionality that is specific to a particular business domain or a particular client application.
The first version shall focus on core framework functions.
Specialized workflows shall be deferred to a later phase unless there is clear demand for them.
Optional features such as richer analytics shall be treated as later-phase items unless they are needed to prove the framework works in a real deployment.
The system shall provide administrators or support staff with dependable maintenance behavior.
The system shall not be targeted at database administrators or power users.
The system shall support tracking items that people already manage in folders, including notes, contacts, references, and project materials.
The system shall support objects in multiple formats and shall not limit objects to one format.
The system shall allow an object to be a document.
The system shall allow an object to be a memo.
The system shall allow an object to be a contact entry.
The system shall allow an object to be an attachment.
The system shall allow an object to be a project-related item that can be linked to other things.
The system shall support associating a note with a person.
The system shall support associating a task with a project.
The system shall support associating a file with a category.
The system shall not force users into one predefined hierarchy.
ZNIX should not infer links too aggressively on its own.
ZNIX should use available metadata to suggest possible links.
ZNIX should use available tags to suggest possible links.
ZNIX should use available names to suggest possible links.
ZNIX should use available user-defined rules to suggest possible links.
The user should make the final decision about links in most cases.
ZNIX should limit or disallow links that would violate basic integrity rules.
ZNIX should disallow links that would create impossible circular structures when such structures are not supported.
ZNIX should disallow links that connect items marked as private or restricted by the user or the organization.
Item changes should feel immediate and consistent.
The system shall keep item views consistent across multiple client applications when the same item is being viewed in more than one client application.
The system shall prioritize correctness over speed when a choice must be made between making a fast wrong change and making a correct change.
At larger scale, the system shall keep responsiveness reasonable for normal searching and browsing.
For everyday work, the user shall still be able to keep moving.
For updates, the framework shall protect consistency first.
The framework may restrict operations when they would be too expensive to do instantly.
Search results may need to be paged or filtered more carefully so users are not overwhelmed with too much at once.
A client that cannot support the full set of features should still be able to work safely with the subset it understands.
A client that cannot support the full set of features must not corrupt or drop shared information.
The system should support graceful degradation for limited clients.
For shared changes and backups, ZNIX should preserve authoritative data in a way that is independent of any single application.
If a feature cannot be represented in a given client, the feature should be preserved as data or metadata rather than lost.
The system shall preserve an item’s relationships and metadata as much as possible when the item changes.
Updating an item shall not require users to rebuild the surrounding organization.
When something is deleted, the system shall handle dependent references predictably.
The system shall apply a user-approved rule for a deleted relationship when such a rule exists.
Backups shall capture both the item and its context.
The physical storage shall preserve the object model.
The storage shall keep identifiers separate from the content itself.
The storage format shall be stable enough that objects can move without losing their links.
When the same item appears in multiple contexts, the system shall remember those relationships.
If dependent references can be repaired, ZNIX shall repair them in a way that is visible and traceable.
If a client only partially understands references, ZNIX shall leave the parts it does not understand untouched and pass them through safely.
The user shall be able to review the suggested link before it becomes part of their organization.
The system shall ask the user before applying a suggested link in general.
The system may automatically apply a suggested link only when the user has explicitly enabled a trusted rule or automation.
The system shall allow the user to undo an automatically applied suggestion.
The system shall show the user why an automatically applied suggestion happened.
The system shall require approval before high-impact links are created unless the user has explicitly said otherwise.
The system shall keep a defined version history for stored items.
The system shall not enforce a hard retention period yet.
The retention policy shall depend on the type of item and storage constraints.
The system shall retain enough history to undo recent changes.
The system shall retain enough history to audit important changes.
The system should support a gentle import path that allows users to bring data in from existing files or applications without reorganizing everything upfront.
The system should allow users to verify that imported items are intact.
The system should allow users to gradually build relationships and hierarchy for imported items inside ZNIX.
The system should support a transition in which users stop relying on the old system for those items.
ZNIX should be the place where archived information is organized and maintained going forward.
The system should usually skip problematic pieces during a partial import.
The system should clearly flag skipped items for later review.
The system should not block the whole migration because that would be too disruptive.
The system should preserve enough detail about skipped items so the user can return later and resolve them.
The system should allow the user to get started with the rest of their information without stopping on unresolved skipped items.
Every meaningful change shall create a recoverable revision.
Deletion shall be reversible through the same history unless the user explicitly chooses a permanent purge or a retention policy has expired.
The system shall keep a trace of what happened for audit or recovery.
A partially compatible client shall be allowed to read and to make only the kinds of changes it fully understands.
ZNIX shall block or isolate anything ambiguous.
If a client does not understand a field, relationship, or object type, it shall not overwrite that data when saving the record back.
ZNIX shall enforce the framework’s validation rules centrally.
ZNIX shall merge updates in a way that does not discard information added by another client.
If a client cannot guarantee safe handling, it shall be limited to read-only or a narrower edit mode.
The system shall make the most common actions obvious right away.
The system shall make common actions feel safe and straightforward so users can start organizing without needing to understand the whole framework first.
The system shall guide users when they create authoritative relationships.
The system shall guide users when they use complex hierarchies.
The system shall guide users when they change shared structures.
The system shall provide guidance or confirmation for advanced actions until users are comfortable.
The system shall not feel restrictive for basic personal use.
ZNIX should explain terms inline when possible.
If a term is optional or advanced, ZNIX may show a brief warning.
ZNIX should not interrupt basic use too heavily just because the language is unfamiliar at first.
The system shall require sign-in for any access to personal data by default.
The system may allow access without sign-in in a deployment that is clearly local and single-user, where the person is already effectively the owner of that environment.
In shared setups, the system shall limit access by ownership or explicitly granted permissions.
The system shall apply ownership or permission-based access restrictions especially for actions that change or expose information to other users or client apps.
The system shall apply stronger checks for destructive actions, sharing, and administrative functions.
Once a user is authenticated, routine viewing may use simpler access checks.
A person shall remain the default owner of their data.
An app shall not receive broader access than the user has explicitly allowed.
If ownership changes or a user no longer controls a space, the system shall immediately stop access and re-check anything that was previously granted through that access.
If an app requests broader access, it shall explain why and obtain explicit consent again instead of silently expanding its scope.
Each service shall have a clearly identified maintainer or owning team to ensure accountability for updates, compatibility, and security fixes.
When the owner of a service changes, ZNIX shall support a clean handoff of the service.
When a service owner changes, the service's metadata, documentation, and any required permissions shall move with the service.
A service owner change shall not break existing clients.
If a service owner becomes unavailable or stops keeping the service current, the service shall be flagged as deprecated or unsupported.
Clients shall be warned before relying on a deprecated or unsupported service.
Service abandonment shall not leave users with a broken or unsafe service without indication that it is no longer maintained.
During the transition period, the system shall keep the service usable if possible.
During the transition period, the system shall provide stronger warnings and may limit changes so users can migrate away without suddenly losing access.
If there are safety or security concerns, the system shall restrict higher-risk operations first.
Clients shall require the user to acknowledge the deprecated or unsupported warning if the user wants to continue.
The system shall impose limits on creating new dependencies for a deprecated or unsupported service.
The system shall discourage new integrations when a safer replacement is available.
The system shall discourage new data writes when a safer replacement is available.
The system shall block immediately any operation that could weaken permissions if the service is no longer trusted.
The system shall block immediately any operation that could make recovery harder if the service is no longer trusted.
The acknowledgement shall not be buried in settings.
The user shall be able to remember the acknowledgement per app and per service for a limited time.
If the user declines, the client shall not proceed with that service.
Personal information is scattered across apps and formats.
Users usually end up locked into the organization imposed by each app.
ZNIX shall provide a common way to store and relate personal information.
The system shall preserve both access and structure when users add items.
Compatible applications shall be able to work with the same underlying information.
The system shall provide a stable object-based framework for storing different kinds of personal information in a consistent way.
The system shall expose services so compatible clients can read the same information store reliably.
The platform should address the frustration caused by data silos and the cost of reworking the same personal information in every application.
The platform should support user portability and continuity.
The system should reduce duplicated data handling.
The system does not yet have specific numeric success targets.
Success should include more compatible applications adopting the framework.
Hard metrics must be confirmed with the product and business teams.
The system shall preserve the structure of contacts, notes, and reference items when users move them from one application to another.
The system shall propagate changes made in one place to everywhere the data is expected to appear.
Success should be measured by fewer support cases related to lost organization or inconsistent copies.
Adoption by client applications is an important success metric.
The system shall enable end users to manage their own information in a way that feels natural to them.
The system shall provide client application developers with a clean service layer for integration.
The system shall support product and support team concerns for usability.
The system shall use framework-specific terms internally for objects and the relationship model.
The system shall keep the concepts simple enough that users can think in terms of items rather than technical storage details.
The system shall balance clarity with implementation accuracy.
The primary users of the ZNIX framework shall be casual individuals who want to store and organize their own information without having to learn a complicated system.
Developers of compatible client applications shall consume the framework services and present the information in their own interfaces.
The exact protocol choice for ZNIX's service layer remains to be finalized.
External systems shall handle authentication if authentication is not built directly into ZNIX.
External systems shall handle backup infrastructure if backup infrastructure is not built directly into ZNIX.
ZNIX shall protect data integrity first.
For unresolved conflict resolution behavior, clients shall receive a clear failure response with enough context to let the user retry or choose between versions.
The system shall support temporary unavailability of some items or operations.
The framework shall expose the current state to client applications.
The system shall support offline behavior in some form.
In offline mode, clients shall be able to continue working on locally available data.
ZNIX shall communicate state changes and availability to client applications through service responses or event notifications.
Client applications shall make state information visible without being disruptive.
Locked items should usually appear read-only or disabled and include a clear reason.
If an action is deferred, the client should tell the user what was queued and whether it may still need confirmation later.
ZNIX shall use precise internal terms for objects, relationships, synchronization state, and access status.
For casual users, ZNIX shall describe the same capabilities in simpler language.
Developer documentation shall use exact terms.
End-user training and support shall focus on what users are trying to do.
Developer guides shall describe state transitions for locked or queued-for-sync items.
Casual users should be able to group related items without needing to understand the underlying object model.
Documentation for developers shall be precise and implementation-oriented.
Developer materials shall describe state behavior so developers can integrate correctly and avoid breaking compatibility.
Documentation for end users shall translate the same topics into task-based guidance.
End-user materials shall include examples that match everyday workflows such as organizing items or restoring from backup.
Any required standards should be chosen to make the framework practical and maintainable.
The system is expected to be subject to data protection and privacy obligations because it handles personal information.
Accessibility should likely be important if the client applications are intended for broad casual use.
The delivery date or release schedule for the ZNIX framework must be verified.
Compatibility with client applications is a major dependency for the ZNIX framework.
Integration work may affect the timeline if the exposed services or data model change.
Resource constraints are likely to matter for the ZNIX framework.
The staffing and rollout plan for the ZNIX framework must be confirmed before they are treated as fixed requirements.
The project shall limit scope so that the core archiving, organizing, and backup workflows are solid before adding additional features.
There is no confirmed release deadline available.
There is no confirmed staffing cap available.
Successful integration with the client applications will affect how quickly the framework can be validated.
The chosen solution should make the framework easy for different client applications to use over time.
The system should use a durable storage approach.
There is no confirmed target release date or staffing limit available.
Any hard milestones or resource constraints must be verified with the project team.
Testing and interface stability shall drive the rollout of the framework.
The system shall keep the core object model and service contracts as stable as possible.
The system shall define clear deprecation periods.
The framework should implement strong access control.
The framework should make users’ personal information available most of the time.
The framework should degrade gracefully during a failure rather than lose data or become unusable.
The framework should include backup, recovery, and maintenance strategies designed to minimize downtime.
The system should make common operations such as opening, finding, and updating items feel responsive to a normal user.
The system should remain responsive even when the data set is fairly large.
The system should use efficient indexing to support the expected responsiveness.
The system should avoid unnecessary loading.
The system should keep service calls lightweight.
The framework shall scale without requiring a redesign when more clients connect or more data is stored.
The storage and service layers shall be modular so that capacity can be improved without breaking the object model or client interfaces.
The design shall avoid single points of failure.
The design shall support gradual growth.
The system shall use transactional updates or another consistency mechanism to prevent partial writes from leaving personal information in a corrupted state.
The system shall provide recovery procedures that restore service without losing confirmed changes.
The system shall include redundancy as part of its fault-tolerance approach.
The system shall include reliable backup recovery as part of its fault-tolerance approach.
Continuous access to the system is important.
The system does not need around-the-clock mission-critical uptime like a banking system.
Users should generally be able to access their information when they need it.
The system should support safe maintenance windows.
The system should have restart or failover procedures that keep the service usable as much as possible.
Users shall be able to limit who or what can see specific items.
Retention rules shall allow data to be deleted or aged out without leaving stray copies behind.
Backups shall be protected with the same or stricter controls as live data.
The framework shall enforce access-control rules centrally so client applications do not implement their own handling.
The service layer shall include authentication and authorization.
The system shall maintain audit logs for changes.
The system shall maintain audit logs for access attempts.
The system shall maintain audit logs for administrative actions so later verification is possible.
The same policy engine shall govern what backup data is copied.
The same policy engine shall govern how long backup data is retained.
The same policy engine shall govern when backup data is securely removed.
Client applications shall request actions.
The service layer shall check policy and either allow or deny requested actions.
The policy engine shall sit behind the service layer so that the same rules apply regardless of which client is used.
The policy engine shall write an audit record whenever it makes a decision.
The policy engine shall write an audit record whenever a protected item is changed.
The audit records shall support review of who did what, when, and under which rule.
The system shall not rely on the client to behave correctly.
Client applications shall not break whenever ZNIX evolves.
Service contracts shall be versioned.
Older interfaces shall be preserved for a reasonable period.
The system shall make additive changes where possible instead of changing existing behavior in place.
Breaking changes shall provide a clear migration path for client developers.
Breaking changes shall provide enough notice for client developers to adapt.
Versioning shall be explicit in the service interface at the API or contract level.
Clients shall be able to target a known stable version.
When a new version is introduced, the older version shall continue to work for a defined transition period.
The system shall provide deprecation notices and release notes that tell developers what changed and what they need to do.
Retiring an old version shall be scheduled and communicated well in advance.
An old version should be retired only after a practical migration path for the main client integrations has been confirmed.
The system shall favor extension over replacement so that new features and richer data models can be added without invalidating existing functionality.
The system shall allow optional fields or new object types.
The system shall change existing structures only when there is a clear benefit that outweighs the migration cost.
If a change risks breaking clients, the system shall handle it as a planned compatibility event with versioning, testing, and a transition period rather than an ad hoc release.
A direct support path shall be available for client developers during the transition window.
The system should be managed to prevent scope creep caused by requests for excessive features and integrations.
The system should enforce strict service contracts and policy rules to avoid inconsistency across client applications.
The system should have strong governance around the core interfaces and data model.
The system should keep changes incremental when managing evolving requirements.
The system should validate changes against a few representative client use cases before expanding them broadly.
A small core group shall own the interface and data model decisions.
The interface and data model decision process shall include input from client developers and operations or support personnel.
The decision process shall be lightweight but explicit.
The system governance shall include documented standards defining what is part of the stable core and what may vary by client or extension.
If there is a disagreement, the core team shall make the final decision.
Before making a final decision in a disagreement, the core team shall review the impact on compatibility, auditability, and long-term maintenance.
The system should feel immediate to users during normal work.
The transition plan shall be very visible and predictable.
The system shall settle prioritization early for enhancements and changes.
The system shall rank enhancements first by how well they support the core information-management use case.
The system shall rank enhancements next by how much risk they add to existing clients.
The system shall rank enhancements finally by how broadly they help multiple applications.
